opener.heading: Week 27: Independence Day Celebration 🎆
about: Everything a party takes, Azlyn makes. A cake out of a cereal box on Friday, streamers on the scooter for Saturday, a real cake iced on Sunday morning and a bag packed for after dark. Monday onward the week runs on what July hands you: a paper vest she wears out of the house, ice melting on the path in six places, lunch she cuts herself, three dollar bills at the market.

Independence Day is Sunday and it gets the full day, from the parade round the block to the first fireworks either child has seen. Tuesday carries the other marker. The book is six months old, so the whole row of handprints comes off the wall, January to June, and a July one goes up beside them, with the same four questions underneath and her old answers read back to her. Kreston turns 13 months on Monday.
azlyn: Cutting her own food. A butter knife through cucumber, tomato and cheese, and the different way each one gives.
Saying what she thinks will happen. Which ice cube goes first, how many seeds are in the watermelon, written down before anyone checks.
Counting past what she can hold. Flags on the street, candles onto a plate, watermelon seeds into a jar in tens.
Testing what she made and mending the part that failed. Three paper pockets, four objects, one stone that stayed in.
Three rules she can recite. She dictates the game rules for the fridge and the market rules in the car, then holds you to both.
you: One-year-olds don't understand birthdays, and that's fine
Pointing and giving are the foundations of conversation
Making something she wears is a different order of pride
Repeating an activity across seasons produces a comparison she can make herself
Involvement predicts eating better than persuasion does
Three rules, repeated forever, beats twenty rules said once
shopping: A cereal box for the cake, and a second one flattened for card
A large paper grocery bag, or brown parcel paper
Colored paper, or plain paper and crayons
Plain paper and card, a stack (labels, pockets, lists, rules)
A butter knife, a blunt knife and a chopping board
Washable non-toxic poster paint and a wide soft brush
A washcloth and a dish towel
Ear defenders, or cotton balls and a woolly hat
A rucksack, a picnic blanket, and a blanket for the floor
Sun cream and a sun hat each
A tray, a large bowl, 2 small bowls and a serving plate
Kitchen scales, if you have them
A jar with a lid, for the seeds
3 one-dollar bills and a small purse or an envelope
A shopping bag she can carry herself
Her scooter, balance bike or trike, and her helmet
A sweater each for Azlyn and Kreston
6–8 old things from round the house: a coin, a photograph, a spoon, a key, a book
4 test objects: a stone, a spoon, a crayon, a toy car
The handprint sheets from January onward, off the wall
A plain sponge, a loaf cake, or 12 bought buns
Heavy cream, cream cheese or thick yogurt, 1 tub
Crackers or grapes for the party snack
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 12 months this week. He walks or is a week off it, drinks from a cup with both hands, and follows a one-step instruction. He turns 13 months on Monday the 5th, and from then he walks, climbs and carries things while he moves.

days.title: A Birthday for a Country
days.prepTonight: Empty a cereal box and stand it on the kitchen table with the colored paper, the masking tape and the marker beside it.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Cake That Never Gets Eaten

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Counting the Flags on the Street

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Guest Who Doesn't Know It's a Party

opening.title: What a Party Needs
steps: Ask her what a party has to have. Write the list in her order, one thing per line, with a small picture beside each.
Tell her the country has a birthday on Sunday and turns 251. Say the number twice and let her do what she likes with it.
Circle everything on the list you could make out of a cereal box. Whatever she circled first is what you build at 9:15.

main.title: The Cake That Never Gets Eaten
materials: Colored paper, or plain paper and crayons
1 pencil, for poking the candle holes
steps: Tape the box shut along every seam and stand it on its end. She tapes, you hold the flaps down.
She tears the colored paper up and tapes it over the box until no cardboard shows. Torn edges look like frosting. Plain paper gets crayoned first.
Cut six paper strips, a hand long. She rolls each one round the pencil, slides it off and tapes it.
Draw a flame on the top of each candle with the marker, then write 251 big on the side.
Poke six holes in the top with the pencil where she points and stand a candle in each, loose enough to fall over.
Sing to it. She blows, you tip the candles flat, she stands them back up. As many times as she asks.
main.tip: Loose candles are the design. One that topples and goes back in gets blown at forty times before Sunday.

outside.title: Counting the Flags on the Street
paras: Go before the heat and walk the streets with the most porches. Count flags: on poles, on porch rails, on car windows, in store doorways. Take her morning list and let her mark a line on the back for each one. She will want bunting to count, so let it count.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and walking or close to it. Stick a few loops of tape and a strip of colored paper to his tray and he will pull them off and wear them for a long while. Keep the rolled candles away from him, because they are the size he puts in his mouth. Let him walk part of the street holding one finger.

second.title: The Guest Who Doesn't Know It's a Party
second.intro: Kreston has never been to a party. Azlyn throws him one, and she runs it.
materials: 1 small real snack: crackers, grapes cut lengthways, or berries
steps: She picks the room and spreads the blanket. Wherever it lands is where the party is.
Teddies round the edge, Kreston in the ring with them. She hands out the six cups and decides who sits by who.
Music on. She carries the cake in from another room and stands it on a low table at the edge of the blanket, back from the edge and where you can see it, while everybody watches her do it.

Sing. She blows the candles down and stands them back up, and you sing again. Four rounds is not too many, and every candle that rolls off the table gets counted back into the cake before the next one.
She shares the snack into the cups, one guest at a time, in the order she chose.
She runs the dancing. The same song twice, and you on the floor for it.
The party ends when she says. Cups collected in, cake up on the shelf where Kreston cannot reach the candles.
second.tip: Sing and blow more than once. The part she is practicing is the ending, and a party that finishes four times gives her four goes at it.

alternatives: Cake and candles on the kitchen table, twenty minutes, nothing else.
A party for one teddy with one cup and one song.
Wrap five things from the toy box in newspaper for her to unwrap.
Paper hats from the leftover colored paper.
outAgain: The café, and let her order the cake herself while you hold Kreston
The park with the shade, if the café is packed for the long weekend
A friend's garden, and take the cardboard cake to show
The store for Sunday's berries, with her carrying the basket
The street with the most flags, counting the ones you missed

aroundWorld.title: What Countries Eat on Their Big Day 🎂
paras: Every country with a national day has a food attached to it. In Norway on the 17th of May the parade belongs to the children, and they eat ice cream and hot dogs all day. In India on the 15th of August families make candy in the orange, white and green of the flag. In Mexico on the 15th of September the dish of the night is chiles en nogada, which carries all three flag colors on one plate.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Norway's answer is ice cream, and the children get it all day long. Have yours at the ten fifteen snack, outside and standing up, and tell her whose idea it was.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Norway's national day parade has no soldiers in it at all. It is schoolchildren, from end to end.

days.krestonPM: He is 12 months and drinks from a cup with both hands, so give him a paper cup with a splash of water and let him be a real guest. He will crawl into the middle and pull the cups over, and that is his part of it. Tell Azlyn that a guest who cannot talk yet joins in with his hands.

insight.headline: One-year-olds don't understand birthdays, and that's fine.
paras: Kreston has no idea the cake means anything. He reads the room instead: the singing, every face turned the same way, the pause before the clapping. Joint attention and anticipation are what a party gives a 12-month-old, and both are worth more to him this year than the idea of a birthday. Watch him look at whoever is loudest, then look at you to check whether loud is good. Azlyn is the one who needs today to mean something, so give her the running of it and give him the noise and the faces. He had his own turn a month ago, and he understood that one about as much as he understands this one.

days.safety: The scissors are adult-only and the paper strips are all they cut today, so put them back out of reach between cuts. The rolled candles are the width of Kreston's throat. Count six onto the cake and six off, and count them again after every blowing round at the party, because the cake sits on a table and he is on the blanket below it. Never leave one on the floor while he is down. Cut grapes lengthways. The flag walk runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Parade She Can Ride In
days.prepTonight: Stand the scooter in the hall with two grocery bags, the clothespins and the tape beside it, and check you have a plain sponge, candles and two pints of berries for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Museum with an Empty Shelf

opening.title: Cutting the Streamers
opening.need: 2 plastic grocery bags · 1 pair of scissors (adult only) · 1 roll masking tape.
steps: Cut the handles and the base off one bag so it becomes a tube. She holds it taut and pulls each strip free.
Cut the tube round and round into strips a finger wide, then do the second bag. She says how long they get.
Tape a bundle to a chair back and let her run past to see them lift. The best bundle goes on the front at 9:15.

main.title: Dressing the Scooter
materials: Her scooter, balance bike, trike, or the stroller
The cut streamers, from two grocery bags
5 playing cards, or pieces of cereal-box card
steps: Tape streamers to both handlebar ends. She says how many go on each side, and she will want them uneven.
Clip a peg to the frame by the back wheel with two cards in it so they clack as the wheel turns, and the same on the other side. On a stroller, clip them against the frame.
Cut a rectangle of paper for the front. She draws her name on it and you tape it on.
Tie the longest streamers to the back of the seat with the string. Nothing goes near the front wheel.
Ride it up the hall. Listen for the cards, tighten the clothespins, tape down whatever flapped loose.
Park it behind a closed door, or up out of Kreston's reach. It stays dressed until Sunday night.
main.tip: Tape everything twice as much as looks necessary.

outside.title: The Test Lap
paras: Helmet on, and take the block at her pace with the stroller behind. This is a rehearsal, so let her stop every time a card comes loose. July mornings are warm by half ten: shaded side, and carry water.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and walking, or a week off it. He follows a one-step instruction now as long as the words never change, so carry the fifth playing card and hand it to him at every stop with the same four words: give it to Azlyn. He holds it out, waits for her hand, and wants another go the moment she takes it. His lidded cup rides in the stroller, because he drinks standing up with both hands on it. Keep every cut strip of grocery bag off the floor.

second.title: The Museum with an Empty Shelf
second.intro: The real museum is at 2:30. She opens her own first, and leaves one gap in it on purpose.
materials: 6–8 old objects: a coin, a photograph, a spoon, a key, a book
Paper cut into label cards, 8 of them
steps: Walk the house hunting for the oldest things in it, asking at each one: is this older than you? The wrong answers make the best conversations.
Line them up on the shelf in her order, oldest first, and leave that order alone.
She dictates a label for each one and you write her words on a card, including the ones that make no sense.
Tape each card in front of its object. She reads the row back from memory, pointing as she goes.
Leave one card blank and tape it at the end of the row. That one gets filled in at the museum.
Take the blank card and the marker at 2:30. She draws the thing she liked best, standing in front of it.
Tape it on the end of the shelf at home and let her give the tour again at bedtime.
second.tip: Write the label in her words even where it is wrong. Spoon from the olden days when Grandad was a baby beats a correct date she never said.

alternatives: Three objects, three labels, on a tray.
Sort the old things by what they are made of instead.
Photograph each object and make a paper catalogue.
A museum of her own toys, and she charges you to come in.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month, blank card in her pocket
The library, if the museum has the holiday crowd in it
The pet shop, which she will treat as a museum anyway
A thrift store, hunting for the oldest thing on the shelves
The park with shade and water
days.krestonPM: Take him in the carrier facing out. He gets the same job as this morning and the same four words: give it to Azlyn. Hand him her blank label card, let him pass it over, let her thank him. Twenty minutes is plenty.

insight.headline: Discovery requires an incomplete set.
paras: A finished row of objects is a thing to look at. A row with one gap in it is a job. Azlyn will walk the museum hunting for the exhibit that fills her blank card, and she will look hard at forty things to choose one, which is far more looking than any instruction from you would buy. Bluma Zeigarnik found the same effect in waiters, who held unpaid orders in mind and lost them the moment the bill was settled. An open task stays live. Leave gaps on purpose: one empty page, one missing piece, one card nobody has written yet.

days.safety: Streamers near the front wheel will wrap and stop it dead, so check the front is clear before every ride. Helmet on, and stay between her and the road at every driveway. Cut grocery bag strips are a suffocation risk for a 12-month-old, so bag the offcuts now. Between rides the dressed scooter parks behind a closed door or up out of his reach, streamers, seat string and all. The coin and the key go above his reach. The test lap runs in full sun: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Fourth of July
days.prepTonight: Stand the cake, the berries and the candles on the counter together, put fresh batteries in the flashlight, and find the ear defenders before bed.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Shady Corner of the Garden

opening.title: Counting Out the Candles
opening.need: 1 box of birthday candles · 1 plate or tray.
steps: Tip the candles onto the tray and let her count them. Count them again together, touching each one.
Tell her the country is 251 today and that 251 candles fit on no cake in this house. Ask how many she wants.
Count her number onto the plate and put the box away. That is what the cake gets at 9:15.

main.title: Two Hundred and Fifty-One Candles
materials: 1 plain sponge, loaf cake, or 12 bought buns
1 tub of cream, cream cheese or thick yogurt
1 pint of strawberries and 1 pint of blueberries
The birthday candles she counted out
steps: Cake onto the tray. She spoons the cream on and spreads it with the blunt knife. Lumpy is correct.
Pull the green tops off the strawberries and let her slice them. Fruit gives under a blunt knife and she needs to feel that.
Stripes of strawberry across the cake with cream showing between them, blueberries in a square in the top left. She places every berry.
She pushes her candles in wherever she wants them, including all in one corner.
Light them once now, sing, and let her blow. Blow out the rest yourself and put the matches back up high.
Stand it beside Friday's cardboard cake and photograph the pair. One gets eaten tonight and one does not.
main.tip: Into the fridge the moment it is photographed. July does bad things to cream on a counter.

outside.title: The Parade Round the Block
paras: Take the block at her speed with the stroller behind, the scooter still dressed and the cards rattling. Wave at anyone on a porch, because on the Fourth they wave back. Go before eleven and carry water.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months. Let him push the empty stroller down the flat stretch with both hands on the bar, which takes him further than he walks alone. Quarter his strawberries lengthways and halve the blueberries.

second.title: The Bag for After Dark
second.intro: Tonight she stays up past dark for the first time she will remember, and the afternoon goes on getting ready.
materials: Ear defenders, or cotton balls and a woolly hat
1 sweater each for Azlyn and Kreston
steps: Spread everything on the floor and let her see the pile before anything moves. Name each thing and what it is for.
She packs the rucksack herself, one item at a time. Blanket at the bottom, sweaters on top, snacks and the cup where she can reach them.
Test the flashlight. Let her work the switch thirty times, and tell her the flashlight is her job tonight.
Ear defenders on, and talk to her through them so she hears what they do. With cotton balls, tuck it under the woolly hat.
Agree a hand signal for too loud and practice it ten times, you first, then her. She gives it tonight and you leave, no discussion.
She draws what she thinks fireworks look like before she has seen any. It goes in the bag and comes out tomorrow.
Talk the spot through: where you sit, how far the car is, where the toilets are. The toy goes in last.
second.tip: Say the leaving plan out loud before you go, and mean it. A three-year-old who knows she can go home will last twice as long as one who suspects she is stuck.

alternatives: Watch from a window or a doorstep, door open behind her.
Pack the bag and spend the rest in the paddling pool.
Flashlight games under a sheet in a dark room.
Chalk fireworks on the path, one for every color she expects.
outAgain: The scooter, still dressed, on a long flat path with no road
Sprinklers or a paddling pool, because it will be hot
A shaded park with a bench for the stroller
Feeding the ducks in the cool hour before dinner
The garden and the hose
days.krestonPM: He is 12 months and has never heard a firework. Put the ear defenders on him for a minute at a time this afternoon so tonight is the second time and not the first. Plan on him asleep against you by the second bang.

insight.headline: Pointing and giving are the foundations of conversation.
paras: Kreston hands you things all day and points at what he cannot reach. Both are him starting a conversation with no words in it: he has something in mind and he wants your attention on it. Packing the bag hands him fifty chances at it. He picks the flashlight up, holds it out, waits for you to take it. Answer every offer out loud with the name of the thing. Babies who point and give a lot at twelve months tend to have bigger vocabularies at two. He chooses, you name, and the word arrives attached to something he cared about first. He will hand you the same sweater five times. Take it the fifth time like the first.

days.safety: Lit candles come nowhere near a walking one-year-old. Put Kreston in the high chair before the matches come out, not on your hip. If there are sparklers tonight they stay in adult hands, and they stay hot long after they go out, so have water to drop them in. July heat is the real risk: water every half hour whether she asks or not, and the parade is an hour of open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. If the paddling pool comes out, Kreston stays within arm's reach of you every second it holds water, and you tip it out before you go back in. Before dark, photograph what she is wearing and write your phone number on her arm.

days.title: The Day After
days.prepTonight: Put the biggest paper bag you own on the table with the crayons and the string, and fill two ice trays and freeze them for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Quietest Books in the House

opening.title: Measuring Her with String
opening.need: String or thick wool, 6 feet · 1 pair of scissors (adult only).
steps: Run the string from her shoulder to her knee and cut it there. That is how long the vest will be.
Take a second piece round her chest and a third round the top of her arm, cutting each one to fit.
Lay the three lengths side by side and let her sort them longest to shortest. They come with you to 9:15.

main.title: The Paper Bag Vest
materials: 1 large paper grocery bag, or brown parcel paper, or a large cereal box flattened
The three lengths of string from this morning
steps: Flatten the bag with the base at the top. Lay the shoulder-to-knee string down the front so she sees where the bottom edge lands.
Cut a neck hole in the base panel and an arm hole in each side, sizing them with the arm string. Cut them bigger than looks right.
Cut straight up the middle of the front, bottom edge to neck hole, so it opens like a vest. Try it on her.
Run masking tape round the neck and both arm holes. Paper tears at a hole first, and taped edges get this thing to Thursday.
The table is hers now: both sides, inside included, every crayon she wants. No paint today and nothing wet.
She wears it out at half ten and she wears it to dinner.
main.tip: Cut it a size too big, so she can get it on without you.

outside.title: Walking on the Shady Side
paras: Cross to whichever side of the street has the trees and stay on it. Put her hand flat on a wall in the sun, then on one in the shade, and let her tell you the difference before you name it. Work out where that shade will be by four.

days.infant: Kreston turns 13 months today. He walks, climbs and carries at the same time now, so fold a square of leftover bag paper into a pad too big to fit in his mouth and let him ferry it from one end of the room to the other. Say happy thirteen months out loud, because nobody else will.

second.title: Pockets That Hold Things
second.intro: The vest has nowhere to put anything, and she has a stone she wants to keep.
materials: 4 test objects: 1 stone, 1 spoon, 1 crayon, 1 toy car
steps: Cut the top off an envelope and tape it to the front of the vest on three sides, top left open. That is pocket one.
She loads it with the stone, then walks, jumps, spins and runs the hall. Watch which bit of tape lets go first.
Fix that bit and nothing else, then send her round again with the same stone.
Pocket two comes from folded paper and pocket three from card. She picks the shapes and where they go, including the back.
Test all three with all four objects, one at a time. She marks a tick or a cross on each pocket with the marker.
Count the ticks. Whichever shape carried the stone is the one she wants three of, so cut the extras and tape them on.
Load every surviving pocket and let her walk the hall with all four objects on her.
second.tip: Let the bad pocket fail the whole way. Reinforcing it before she tests it saves the envelope and costs her the information.

alternatives: One pocket, one stone, ten minutes, then the garden.
Tape pockets onto a paper bag and make it a satchel.
Count how many of her real clothes have pockets.
Draw round the four test objects and cut pockets to match.
outAgain: The woods loop, for the shade and the cool under the trees
The stream or the paddling pool, if the woods are too far in this heat
The park at five, when the slide has cooled down
A slow stroller walk with her scootering ahead
The garden with the hose, and nothing else planned
days.krestonPM: At 13 months he climbs onto whatever is knee height, and the woods are full of things at knee height. Let him do the low log with a hand held rather than carrying him past it. Azlyn will want him in a vest too, so tape a spare pocket to his shirt.

insight.headline: Making something she wears is a different order of pride.
paras: She will stop the mail carrier to show him the vest, and she will ask to sleep in it. Azlyn builds her sense of herself out of two things: what she can do, and what belongs to her. A thing she made that then sits on her body lands in both piles at once, which a drawing on the fridge never manages. Expect her to defend it from Kreston harder than she defends any toy, because the toy came from a store and this came out of her hands. Let her wear it out of the house, creased and torn, all week.

days.safety: The scissors come out three times today. Put them on a shelf between cuts, not on the arm of the sofa. The stone and the toy car are choking size for a 13-month-old who walks over and picks things up, so count the four test objects back into a bowl at the end. If the afternoon goes to the stream or the paddling pool, Kreston stays within arm's reach of you every second he is near the water, and you tip the pool out before you go in. Shade takes the heat off and leaves the burn, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Ice in July
days.prepTonight: Check the two ice trays are frozen solid, stand the saucers and the chalk by the back door, and dig out the six handprint sheets from January onward.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Same Trees, Six Months On

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Bowl of Water and the Cups

opening.title: Six Chalk Circles
steps: Go out before the heat and ask her for six places that differ: full sun, deep shade, grass, the doorstep, a dark stone, the wall.
She stands a saucer down at each one, and you draw round it in chalk and number the circles one to six.
Ask which circle will empty first. Write her answer on the path in chalk and leave it where you can both read it later.

main.title: The Ice That Won't Last
materials: 2 trays of ice cubes, frozen overnight
The 6 saucers or jar lids, already out on the circles
The kitchen clock, or a timer on your phone
Paper and 1 marker, for the results
steps: Carry one tray out under the dish towel. She puts a cube on each saucer in number order, drying her hands between them.
Write the time at the top of the paper and set the timer for ten minutes.
Check all six at every buzz. She calls out which are shrinking and you write it down against the numbers.
Between checks, give her the bowl of warm water and a spare cube from the second tray. That one vanishes in a minute and keeps her out there.
Write 1st, 2nd and 3rd on the paper as each circle empties, and let her be the one who calls it.
Read her eight o'clock prediction back to her at the end, and chalk a tick beside it if she called it right.
main.tip: Ten minutes is a long time at three. Set the timer where she can press it herself and give her the chalk between buzzes.

outside.title: The Same Trees, Six Months On
paras: Walk the route from Day 1 and stop under the same trees. In January they were bare, and the book called them sleeping. Ask her what she would call them now. Today the shade under them is a different temperature from the sidewalk, and she can stand with one foot in each. Take the photo from the January spot.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months. Keep the ice cubes away from him. Set the bowl of warm water on the grass in front of him and let him slap it. He will carry the empty saucers to you one at a time if you ask.

second.title: Her Hand Next to January's
second.intro: January's handprint went up on Day 1 and one has gone up every month since. July's makes seven of twelve, made the same way, with the same four questions under it.
materials: The six handprint sheets from January onward, or the photos of them
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Get all six earlier sheets out first and lay them in a row, January at one end. Ask whether any of those hands looks like her hand, and let her hold her palm over January's and over June's.
Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping it. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up onto the thick paper.
Washcloth in your hand before she lifts, and wipe her down where she stands.
Do Kreston's beside hers on the same sheet while he is calm.
Write July and the date under both prints with the marker. Seventh of twelve. The six earlier sheets go back up on the wall in order, and the new one tapes up at the end of the row.
Ask the four questions from Day 1 again and write her answers word for word on the second sheet: favorite color, favorite food, favorite song, what she wants to do this year.
Read her January answers back to her after. She will disagree with herself, which is the best part of it.
second.tip: She will want a second print. Let her, on the third sheet, and get the first one out of reach before she improves it.

alternatives: Draw round her hand in pencil and skip the paint.
Feet as well, on the doorstep, hosed off after.
Ask the four questions on video instead.
Print both children's hands onto a paper bag and use it as a gift bag.
outAgain: Swimming, and the pool is the coolest room in town today
An outdoor pool, if the indoor one is packed
The paddling pool at home with the hose
A shaded splash pad
The library, for an hour of cool air and a book each
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool too, and a hand stays on him from the changing room to the water every time, including the two steps to the bench. At 13 months he walks, and poolside is the worst floor in the building for a new walker. In the pool he wants to be upright and moving, so the shallow steps are where he will spend the hour. Keep him inside arm's reach the whole time and get him out before he goes cold.

insight.headline: Repeating an activity across seasons produces a comparison she can make herself.
paras: Azlyn will put her palm down on January's outline without being asked, and the gap round the edge of it is the whole lesson. One handprint is a keepsake for you. Seven, made the same way across seven months, are evidence she can read without being told what to think. Same paint, same brush, same four questions, same size of sheet, so the only thing that changed is her. Keep the method identical every time, even where you can see a better way to do it, because a bigger sheet or a different paint gives her a difference she cannot pin on herself. By December she will guess the gap before the paint comes out.

days.safety: Ice cubes are a choking hazard for a 13-month-old and half of them end up on the ground, so count them out and sweep before he is down. The warm-water bowl at nine and the bowl of water at quarter past four are standing water at his height, so Kreston stays inside arm's reach of you while either one is full, and you tip them out when she has finished. Swimming needs eyes on both children for the whole hour, both of them inside arm's reach, and the phone stays in the bag. July sun burns faster than it feels: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Azlyn Makes Lunch
days.prepTonight: Stand the watermelon on the counter where she will see it first thing, put the corn and the chopping board out, and move the big knife out of reach.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Everything She Can Cut with a Butter Knife

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Library Book Nobody's Read Yet

opening.title: Pulling the Husks Off
opening.need: 2 corn on the cob · 1 large bowl · 1 saucepan.
steps: Give her both cobs and the bowl and let her strip the green husks off. Show her once, then leave her with it.
The silk is the long job. Every thread comes off, and she will hunt them for twenty minutes.
Stand the bare cobs in the saucepan of cold water on the back of the stovetop, ready for noon.

main.title: Everything She Can Cut with a Butter Knife
materials: The 2 husked corn on the cob
1 pot of yogurt, 1 lemon, olive oil, salt
steps: Cucumber onto the board first, because it gives without a fight. Show her one cut, hand over the butter knife, and step back. Cut pieces go into a bowl as she works.
Tomatoes next. The skin resists and then goes all at once, and she needs to feel that. Cheese in slabs, bread torn.
Dip: yogurt into a bowl, half the lemon squeezed in, a spoon of oil, a pinch of salt. She stirs, tastes, and says what it needs.
Corn onto the stovetop at twenty past eleven, so the water is boiling by half past and the cobs have their ten minutes before noon. You stand at the pan, she stays the other side of the counter.
She lays the whole lot out on the serving plate however she wants. Say nothing about the arrangement.
It goes on the table at noon and nobody rearranges it, including you.
main.tip: Cucumber, tomato, soft cheese and bread all give way to a butter knife. Banana and boiled egg will do the same job next week.

outside.title: What's Ripe on This Street
paras: July is the month the street starts producing. Walk it looking at what is growing where: tomatoes going red in pots, blackberries still hard and green, apples the size of marbles, zucchini under leaves. Ask which ones you could eat today. If a neighbor is out, let her ask them.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and wants to be at the counter with everyone else. Give him the thick end of the cucumber, too big to choke on and cold on gums that are working hard this month, and let him gnaw it in the high chair beside her. Hand him the empty bowl to carry after.

second.title: One Whole Watermelon
second.intro: One watermelon takes the whole afternoon: weighed, guessed at, opened, counted, eaten outside.
materials: Kitchen scales, if you have them
1 jar with a lid, for the saved seeds
Chalk, or paper and a crayon, for the guesses
steps: Let her lift it first. Weigh it on the scales, or pass it round and see who holds it out longest. Write the weight in chalk.
Guesses: how many seeds are in it? Write hers, write yours, put one down for Kreston. Nobody changes their answer later.
Cut it on the tray with her standing back where she can see, and put the big knife out of reach before anyone touches a piece.
Everyone eats outside, spoons only, seeds spat onto the tray. This mess hoses off.
Count the seeds into the jar in tens, out loud, and let her decide whose guess was closest.
Lid on the jar and onto the windowsill. Those get planted in the spring.
Fill the bowl at the tap and float the rind halves in it. They sit like boats and she will push them round until dinner.
second.tip: Let her spit the seeds. The tray catches all of it.

alternatives: Half a melon, spoons, on the back step, nothing counted.
Freeze the leftover chunks on a tray for tomorrow.
Rind boats in the paddling pool instead of a bowl.
Sort the seeds into tens on a plate.
outAgain: The library, and let her carry the returns bag in herself
The bookstore or a thrift store, if the library is shut this week
Indoor playground, if the heat has beaten everybody
The park with the shade and the water fountain
A café with cool air and the new book
days.krestonPM: He gets watermelon scraped to a mush with a spoon, no chunks and no seeds near him. At the library, put him down in the board book corner and let him pull books off the low shelf. He will bring one back to you over and over, so take it every time and read the first page.

insight.headline: Involvement predicts eating better than persuasion does.
paras: The cucumber she cut is a cucumber she eats. Children who handle, wash, cut and serve food eat more of it and try new things sooner. Handling wears the strangeness off, and she has had this cucumber in both hands since a quarter past nine. By noon she has smelled the lemon, felt the tomato give under the knife and tasted the dip twice while stirring, so what arrives at the table is a known thing that belongs to her. Say nothing about eating it. A three-year-old who made lunch and is then encouraged to eat it hears pressure instead of an invitation.

days.safety: The big knife is adult-only, it cuts the melon once, and it goes back out of reach before anybody eats. Watermelon chunks and seeds are choking size for Kreston at 13 months, so his portion gets scraped to a mush. The rind bowl, the afternoon dishpan and the paddling pool if it comes out are standing water at his height, so Kreston stays within arm's reach of you whenever any of them is full, and you tip them out the moment she has finished with them. The corn pan is boiling water at her head height: handle turned in, and she stays the other side of the counter while it is on. Kreston goes in the high chair for the twenty minutes the pan is up, because the corn runs through free play and he walks. The street walk is forty-five minutes of July sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Three Rules
days.prepTonight: Put the card, the marker and a ball by the back door, and find three one-dollar bills and something she can use as a purse.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Game That Goes on the Fridge

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Money in Her Own Pocket

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Playing the Game on Her Own

opening.title: What Makes It a Game
opening.need: 1 ball · a clear bit of floor.
steps: Play a game she knows, rolling the ball between you, and stop halfway through on purpose.
Play it again with no rules for one minute: ball anywhere, score whenever you like, both at once. Let it get daft and let her complain.
Ask what was wrong with that. Her answer is what you build the new game out of.

main.title: The Game That Goes on the Fridge
materials: 1 piece of card, or the back of a cereal box
steps: Ask her to invent a game and let it run long and mad. Take every rule she says, including the ones about dragons.
Play it once through as she described it. It falls apart somewhere, and that collapse is the material for the hour.
Cut it down to three. Say them back as a list: you have to do this, you can't do that, this is how you win. Let her correct you until it matches.
Write the three rules on the card in marker, with a picture beside each so she can read them back without you.
Take the chalk out and mark what the game needs on the ground: a start line, a target, a place to stand.
Tape the card to the fridge at her height. It stays there for the summer and anyone can play it.
main.tip: Write her words, not the tidy version. A rule she can recite is a rule she will enforce on you at dinner.

outside.title: Chalking It Out Full Size
paras: Take the chalk and the ball to the biggest flat surface you can reach on foot and draw the game out full size: the line, the target, a box for each player. Play it five times, and anyone walking past gets asked to join.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months, walks, and carries things while he moves, which makes him a useful ball fetcher. Give him that job out loud and let Azlyn be the one who hands it to him. If she wants one of the three rules to be about him, write it down.

second.title: The Money in Her Own Pocket
second.intro: The market is at two thirty and she is going in with three dollar bills that belong to her and a list she can read.
materials: Paper and crayons, for the picture list
1 small purse, an envelope, or the vest pocket
1 shopping bag she can carry herself
steps: Decide together what she is buying. Three things, and she draws each one on the paper however she likes.
Write the word beside each drawing in marker, so a stallholder can read it over her shoulder if she goes shy.
Count the three bills into her hand, then into the purse. Open and shut it ten times, because a purse she fumbles gets handed to you.
Agree the three market rules out loud in her words: hold the bag, hands off the fruit unless we are buying it, stay where you can see me.
Rehearse the asking. You be the stallholder, four times, until can I have one please comes out without a run-up.
She packs the bag herself: the list, the purse, nothing else.
At the market she hands the money over and takes the change back into her purse while you stand behind her.
second.tip: Let her count the money out at her own speed and let the line wait.

alternatives: A store instead of a market, one item, same three bills.
A stall at home, and she sells you the fruit bowl.
Draw the list and skip the trip if the heat is brutal.
Sort a jar of coins into piles by size.
outAgain: The market, and she buys her three things herself
The produce market or a farm stand, if the market packs up by three
The park after, with whatever fruit she bought
A bakery, and let her choose and pay for one thing
Home to the garden, and a picnic of the shopping
days.krestonPM: Keep him in the carrier or strapped into the stroller at the market. At 13 months he points at everything he wants and he can reach a fruit display from a stroller, so park side-on. Name what he points at every time, even the fortieth.

insight.headline: Three rules, repeated forever, beats twenty rules said once.
paras: Azlyn holds about three pieces of information at a time, and a loud market takes that down to two. Twenty careful instructions in the car are gone before the door shuts. The card on the fridge works for the same reason the market rules do: three items, the same words every time, a picture she can read without you. She will start reciting them at you, correcting your version, enforcing them on Kreston, and the rule leaves your mouth for good. Resist the fourth. Each one you add pushes another out, and the one that falls off is never the one you would have chosen.

days.safety: Her change comes back as coins, and a coin is a choking hazard for a 13-month-old who walks over and picks things up, so the purse lives in her pocket or your hand and every coin goes straight back into it. The market means traffic, a crowd and a curb: say the three rules before you get out of the car, not on the sidewalk, and keep a hand on the stroller brake while she pays. The full-size game runs on open ground at half past ten, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.
